li.a: BBC History: Michael Stone kills three at IRA funerals
RTE News: Gibraltar killings led to shocking series of events
The Irish News: Documentary to explore 1988 Milltown cemetery killings
BBC News: Stone convicted of SF murder bids

content.p: On 16 March 1988, as three coffins were being lowered into a shared grave at Milltown Cemetery in west Belfast, a lone loyalist gunman opened fire on the crowd and threw hand grenades. Michael Stone, a member of the Ulster Defence Association, killed three people and wounded dozens more before a crowd of mourners caught him on the motorway just beyond the cemetery fence. Television crews filmed the attack, and the pictures of a bearded man jogging through the cemetery, firing at mourners, went round the world.

The funeral of one of Stone's victims then led to a second killing within three days. BBC History calls the 14 days that began with the shootings in Gibraltar and ended with the killing of two soldiers one of the darkest periods of the Troubles.

The three people being buried, Mairéad Farrell, Daniel McCann and Seán Savage, were killed by the SAS in Gibraltar on 6 March 1988. RTE reported that they were suspected of preparing a bomb attack on the changing of the guard at the governor's residence. They were unarmed, and no bomb was found in their car. A coroner's jury in Gibraltar found the killings lawful, but in 1995 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the families' right to life had been infringed. A Thames Television documentary, Death on the Rock, had meanwhile reported eyewitness accounts that the three were shot without any attempt to arrest them.

Officials in Belfast had warned of "the likelihood of emotional or difficult scenes" when the bodies came home. For years the policing of IRA funerals had been a grievance: large numbers of security personnel in riot gear at earlier services had provoked strong complaints from republicans, even though the authorities thought they were needed to stop volleys being fired over coffins. BBC History says that after negotiations with Catholic church leaders the police and army agreed to scale back and keep a low profile, watching from the sidelines instead of flanking the cortege.

That arrangement mattered later. Sinn Fein argued that there must have been collusion with the security forces, since only a small number of people knew in advance that the police presence would be reduced. The UDA and its fighting wing, the UFF, denied sanctioning the attack but stopped short of condemning it, BBC History says, and Stone said he acted alone.

According to CNN, Stone was born in 1955, although the exact date is unclear, and grew up in the Braniel estate in Protestant east Belfast. He joined the Tartan Gang at 13 and was an active UDA member by 16. He had already served a prison term in Crumlin Road jail for firearms possession when he planned the cemetery attack. He later described living a double life, rubbing dirt into his clothes so that those close to him would think he had been working as a builder.

He said his provocation was the IRA bombing of a Poppy Day memorial service at Enniskillen, which had killed 11 people. BBC History says the Sinn Fein leaders he claimed were the targets of his attack were Gerry Adams, Martin McGuinness and Danny Morrison. Years afterwards he said he had thought of his victims as targets and "dehumanized" them.

BBC History says it is unclear whether he knew how lightly the funeral was policed, but he chose to mingle with the mourners. It says he attended the service at St Agnes church, taking a seat near the Sinn Fein leaders, and then joined the procession to the republican plot, having reasoned that striking in the church would make escape almost impossible.

A large crowd was present, among them Adams and McGuinness, according to CNN. The first shot was taken by some mourners for an IRA salute, BBC History says, but a second followed, along with a grenade, just as the last of the three coffins was being lowered into the joint grave. Mourners took cover behind gravestones.

Many in the crowd chased Stone as he retreated. As Adams appealed for calm over a loudhailer, BBC History says, Stone kept firing and throwing grenades at his pursuers. All three of his victims died during the pursuit. Thomas McErlean was 20, married with two children. John Murray was 26, a married father of two. Both were civilians. The third victim was an IRA member, named by BBC History as Kevin Brady and by The Irish News as Caoimhín Mac Brádaigh.
The count of injured varies: RTE says 50, BBC History says "over fifty", and CNN says 60, including pensioners and children.

Mourners caught Stone just beyond the cemetery fence, on the motorway. He was disarmed and beaten before the police arrived and arrested him. CNN reports that RUC officers dragged him to safety and arrested him, and that without them he would have been killed by the crowd. It says he still walks with a slight limp from the dislocated thigh bone he suffered.

Kevin Myers of the Irish Times wrote, in words BBC History quotes, that unarmed young men had charged a man hurling grenades and firing an automatic pistol, and that Victoria Crosses had been won for less. Northern Ireland Secretary Tom King strongly condemned the attack and appealed for calm.

During Mac Brádaigh's funeral, three days after the attack, two British Army corporals, Derek Wood and David Howes, in plain clothes and a civilian car, drove into the middle of the cortege. RTE says they did so by mistake. Following Stone's attack, some mourners believed they were loyalists attempting another one. A crowd surrounded the car and dragged the men out, and television filmed it. The corporals were taken away and shot dead by the IRA.

Margaret Thatcher later told Taoiseach Charlie Haughey, in a meeting recorded by Irish officials, that she would never forget receiving the bodies of the two soldiers and that their relatives had seen the films. The British government was criticised over how long the security forces took to intervene. King said the RUC had believed there were no soldiers in the area and that an army helicopter took time to establish what was happening. The DUP's Peter Robinson accused the Chief Constable of "abdicating" policing to the IRA in west Belfast, which King denied.

Stone was convicted of the Milltown deaths, three earlier killings and other offences. Accounts of the sentence differ. BBC History says he received a number of life sentences, and CNN says a minimum of 30 years for six murders and five attempted murders. CNN adds that he pleaded not guilty and refused to speak at his trial. BBC News says he admitted the other three murders. The CNN account identifies those three as Catholics shot dead between 1984 and 1987.

He served his sentence in the Maze prison, and CNN says he became an icon to die-hard loyalists; to republicans, it says, he was a demon. He was released in 2000 under the Good Friday Agreement, after 12 years by CNN's count. BBC History calls the release extremely controversial. He backed the agreement and met the Northern Ireland secretary Mo Mowlam in 1998, and published an autobiography, None Shall Divide Us, in 2004. He told the BBC he did not regret any fatalities, because the operations had been "military operations".

In November 2006 Stone went to the Stormont parliament buildings on the day Ian Paisley and Martin McGuinness were to be nominated as Northern Ireland's first and deputy first ministers. He denied the charges and said it was performance art, but a judge at Belfast Crown Court called that "wholly unconvincing". BBC News reports that the court heard he pointed an imitation gun at a security guard and ignited a device in a flight bag, which failed to explode, and that he carried seven nail bombs, three knives, a hatchet and a garrotte. The judge, Mr Justice Deeny, noted that Stone had repeatedly told police when arrested that he meant to kill Adams and McGuinness, and had posted letters to two journalists saying so.
He was convicted of attempting to murder them and of seven other charges, and BBC History says he was sentenced to 16 years.

The funerals of March 1988 are still a subject of documentary study. In 2018 the BBC scheduled The Funeral Murders, a film by Vanessa Engle with previously unheard testimony, which the director said showed how enduring conflict arises when groups hold politically polarised views.
